title: A 13-Year-Old Just Swam Faster Than Almost Anyone on Earth
summary:
Imagine being 13 years old and standing on a podium at the Asian Games. That's exactly where Yu Zidi of China was this week — for the third time!

Yu swam the 400m individual medley (a race where swimmers use four different strokes: butterfly, backstroke, breaststroke and freestyle). She led from the very first splash to the final touch. Her time? Four minutes 28.56 seconds — a brand-new Asian Games record. The old record had lasted since 2014, and she beat it by nearly 4.5 seconds. That's like winning a race by a whole swimming pool length.

She finished almost 4 seconds ahead of the next swimmer, her teammate Ke Wenxi. Japan's Mio Narita took bronze.

This was Yu's third gold in Nagoya, Japan. She already won the 200m butterfly and the 200m individual medley — both in record times too. Only one swimmer in the whole world has gone faster than her this year: Summer McIntosh of Canada.

People are already whispering about the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics. Not bad for someone who can't even drive yet!
why_it_matters: It shows that being young doesn't stop you from being world-class — practising something step by step, whether it's swimming or maths or music, can put you on the podium.

background_read: The Asian Games (a huge sports competition held every four years for athletes from countries all across Asia) is one of the biggest sporting events in the world after the Olympics.
In an individual medley, swimmers must use four strokes in a set order: butterfly, backstroke, breaststroke and freestyle.
Summer McIntosh (a Canadian teenager who has already won Olympic gold medals) is one of the very few swimmers faster than Yu, which shows how young the sport's top stars have become.
Article_Structure: WHO: Yu Zidi, a 13-year-old swimmer from China, racing against her teammate Ke Wenxi and Mio Narita of Japan.
WHAT: She won the 400m individual medley in 4 minutes 28.56 seconds — a new Asian Games record — leading from the first splash to the final touch.
WHERE: The Asian Games in Nagoya, Japan, where she had already won the 200m butterfly and 200m individual medley.
WHY: She beat a record that had stood since 2014 by nearly 4.5 seconds, finished almost 4 seconds ahead of the next swimmer, and is now being talked about for the 2028 Olympics.

perspectives.description: They are excited that Yu has won three golds at only 13, all in record times, beating swimmers years older than her.
Some people question whether very young athletes should train at such a hard, top level, in case they get injured or tired of the sport.
The rest of the swimmers are racing against someone almost a decade younger, and the gap of nearly 4 seconds shows how far ahead she is.
